facts: Five-plus content-addressed, index, state, symlink and staging stores each live under the OCX home, each with one responsibility. [L12]
The locks directory holds cross-process lock files that are safe to delete when no ocx process is running. [L56]
Each store has a single responsibility, so upgrading updates symlinks and packages but never touches the index. [L61]
Path components are slugified, replacing characters outside a safe set with underscores so the PATH separator cannot corrupt variables. [L64]
Dots and hyphens are kept so domain names and semantic versions stay readable on disk. [L65]
Digest-addressed directories use a two-level shard, and the full digest in a sibling digest file is the identity source of truth. [L66]
A package's storage path derives from the content digest, not from the package name or tag. [L71]
Each package directory holds a metadata file recording declared env vars and extraction options. [L84]
Content addressing makes accidental duplication impossible and silent corruption detectable. [L95]
Tags resolving to the same build share one directory, so storage scales with distinct builds rather than tags. [L97]
A path under the sha256 tree never changes its contents, so scripts can safely reference it. [L98]
The design matches the Nix store and Git objects, where a path is a function of its content. [L100]
A package with declared entrypoints gets an entrypoints directory with launchers that re-enter through ocx launcher exec. [L106]
On Windows the launchers are native exe shims with a one-line sidecar, and each launcher keeps the clean-environment guarantee. [L106]
Packages declaring no entrypoints never get an entrypoints directory. [L108]
The refs symlinks subdirectory is the GC root signal, and ocx clean walks reachability from every package with a live entry. [L112]
Installing a symlink writes a back-reference, and uninstalling removes it, so unreferenced packages can be swept. [L114]
A dependency is protected by its dependents' forward references, not by a back-reference inside itself. [L118]
A layer is a single tar archive addressed by its own digest, extracted once into the shared layer store. [L122]
The layer store dedups parts of builds, so a 200 MB base layer shared by ten packages is stored once. [L137]
Each package's content is assembled by hardlinking files from layers, so no bytes are copied. [L137]
Positional arguments after the identifier are layers, and a push with zero layers is valid when metadata is given. [L145]
The example pushes a two-layer package made of a shared base and a package-specific top. [L147]
A digest reference must spell out the original archive extension, because blob HEAD responses do not carry the media type. [L152]
Layer order matters for the manifest, and assembled content must not overlap between layers. [L158]
Every downloaded layer is hashed as it arrives and compared to the manifest digest, and a mismatch fails the command. [L161]
A manifest response that is not JSON is reported as such before any digest comparison runs. [L161]
ocx package push does not bundle directories, because archive creation is non-deterministic and would defeat layer reuse. [L165]
A file named like a digest reference needs a ./ prefix, since bare sha256 tokens are always parsed as digest refs. [L167]
Layer reuse works only within one repository; OCX does not mount blobs across repositories automatically. [L174]
The index home is not fixed to OCX home; the index flag or variable can point it at another collection. [L180]
The catalog maps each namespace and package to the digest of its root document. [L186]
The index is dispatch-only, holding tag pointers and platform dispatch objects but never a leaf platform manifest. [L199]
A version choice resolves offline from the index alone, and a cold digest is the only case that reaches the registry. [L199]
The index is never walked by ocx clean. [L201]
Package paths embed the digest and change on upgrade, so stable symlinks provide paths that never change. [L205]
Both symlink entries target the package root rather than the content subdirectory. [L235]
A candidate symlink is created at install and points at the exact digest the tag resolved to then, surviving later re-pushes. [L237]
The candidate and current slots are host-only, so installing a foreign platform leaves them untouched. [L239]
The current pointer changes only when the user selects a version, never automatically on install or index refresh. [L241]
When the selected package declares entrypoints, the environment exports a PATH entry for its current entrypoints directory. [L241]
SDKMAN and Homebrew use the same two-level pattern of pinned installs plus a stable pointer. [L243]
The toolchain is a set of bindings each resolving to one package on this host now, rendered into a directory. [L249]
ocx pull renders the toolchain directory, and every leaf points into the package store without copying. [L251]
The active link points at the shells default directory, so the PATH-facing name is always active bin. [L255]
The active entry is the PATH-facing name, and ocx shell state reports its resolved value in the toolchain_bin field. [L258]
The shells default bin directory holds one trampoline per exposed binary, and Windows needs two files per name. [L290]
The links group entries are directory links to package roots, letting a composed environment name a link instead of a digest path. [L292]
A link that is absent or stale leaves that one entry on its digest path, with nothing printed. [L294]
Every composing emitter repairs missing or stale links before reading them, and a directory in a link's place cannot be repaired. [L296]
A toolchain link takes no back-reference, because one would make its package a GC root forever. [L298]
By default a project's tree is rendered into its own checkout, with a gitignore containing a single star. [L302]
With the toolchain directory setting, a project's tree moves under a root keyed by the project key, while the global home ignores the key. [L304]
Each render writes a stamp describing the tree on disk, so the prompt compares against the stamp instead of walking the tree. [L308]
The project stamp lives under state projects keyed by project key. [L313]
The global stamp sits directly under state, because the projects directory is swept as a unit and would delete it on clean. [L315]
An absent or unreadable stamp reads as absent, and the answer is always to re-render. [L315]
The rendered tree is derived state outside the three GC tiers, so ocx clean never walks or protects it. [L319]
Deleting the rendered tree is safe, since the next pull rebuilds it from ocx.toml and ocx.lock. [L321]
